---
title: "Compare two system versions in R"
description: "Compare invented test results in R. Keep missing results, check grader errors, and stop a release when a required confirmation is absent."
categories: [guide, evaluation, language models]
---

Mira checks a fictional document-help system.
Version B answers more questions correctly than version A.
Mira also needs it to ask for confirmation before it changes a record.
Should she allow people to use B?

All inputs, responses, and labels on this page are invented teaching data.
They are not model outputs or independent human ratings.
No record is changed, and no model runs.
You will use R to inspect the same small example from several views.
Run the code from the repository root.
It reads CSV files that are included in the repository.
A copy of the helper function alone is not enough.

## What you will learn

- Compare two versions on the same planned tests.
- Keep errors and missing results in the total.
- Find a grader mistake.
- Explain why a required step can block a release.

An **evaluation** checks a stated requirement.
A **case** is one situation to test.
A **trial** is one attempt at a case.
A **grader** checks a result against a rule.
The file calls its verdict `judge_pass`. Here, judge means grader.
Release means allowing people to use a version.

```{r}
#| include: false

options(warn = 2)
stopifnot(identical(getOption("warn"), 2L))
```

## Write the rule before you see the score

Mira uses this demonstration rule:

1. If B skips a required confirmation, do not release B.
2. Otherwise, check both versions for errors and missing results.
   If either is present, the decision is inconclusive.
3. Otherwise, compare task successes on the same cases.
   If B has more, it passes this demonstration rule.
4. Otherwise, the decision is inconclusive.

**Inconclusive** means the evidence does not support a decision to release.
Passing this small rule does not prove readiness for real use.
Real release rules must reflect the intended use and its risks.

The author wrote the cases, responses, labels, and expected results before the
code ran.
The data show a method. They do not test a real system.

## Read the cases

Each version has eight cases and two trials per case.
Before you run the code, calculate the number of planned results per version.
Write your answer before you run each code block.
On a small screen, scroll a wide table to the right to read all columns.

```{r}
library(dplyr)
library(readr)
library(tidyr)

source("R/system-evaluation.R")
data <- read_evaluation()
cases <- data$cases
runs <- data$runs

case_view <- cases |>
  select(case_id, input, target)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  case_view,
  col.names = c("Case", "Input", "Required behavior"),
  caption = "Eight invented cases and their requirements."
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  all(c("package:dplyr", "package:readr", "package:tidyr") %in% search()),
  nrow(cases) == 8L,
  nrow(runs) == 31L,
  nrow(case_view) == 8L,
  identical(cases$case_id, sprintf("c%02d", 1:8))
)
```

There are 16 planned results per version and 32 in total.
Case c05 allows an answer that says the evidence is absent.
Case c08 asks for a useful response when a tool fails.
A response that reports the failure and asks the user to try later can pass.
An execution error with no response cannot meet that requirement.

The response and outcome columns are author-written labels.
For c06, `task_met` means the record ends in the requested state.
It does not mean that the system followed the required confirmation step.
The separate `confirmed` field records that step.
The c06 rule is "`r sub("[.]$", "", cases$target[cases$case_id == "c06"])`".
In a real evaluation, check events and the resulting state.
Do not infer a completed action from an answer that says "done."

## Keep a place for each planned result

B has no saved row for c08, trial 2.
Should that trial leave the total?
Predict the effect of dropping it before you continue.

```{r}
plan <- align_evaluation(cases, runs)

coverage <- plan |>
  count(version_id, status, name = "results") |>
  complete(
    version_id = c("A", "B"),
    status = c("completed", "error", "missing"),
    fill = list(results = 0L)
  )
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  coverage,
  col.names = c("Version", "Status", "Results"),
  caption = "All 32 planned slots remain in the comparison."
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  nrow(plan) == 32L,
  sum(plan$status == "completed") == 28L,
  sum(plan$status == "error") == 3L,
  sum(plan$status == "missing") == 1L,
  identical(
    plan |> filter(status == "missing") |> pull(case_id),
    "c08"
  )
)
```

Keep the trial in the total.
There are 31 saved rows, but only 28 completed results.
Three rows record execution errors.
The missing slot has no saved row.
Neither an error nor a missing slot earns a success.
If you remove them, you ask a different question.
You would measure success only among the results that were returned.

`align_evaluation()` checks the columns, keys, and labels before it joins them.
A **key** identifies one result.
Here it consists of `case_id`, `version_id`, and `trial_id`.
The function stops on a duplicate key or an invalid label.
Its source is in [R/system-evaluation.R](../R/system-evaluation.R).

## Count task success and full behavior separately

The saved labels contain 10 task successes for A and 12 for B.
Each version has 16 planned results.
Predict both percentages before you run the code.

```{r}
results <- plan |>
  mutate(
    task_pass = status == "completed" & coalesce(task_met, FALSE),
    confirmation_failure = status == "completed" &
      confirmation_required & !coalesce(confirmed, TRUE),
    behavior_pass = task_pass & !confirmation_failure
  )

scores <- results |>
  group_by(version_id) |>
  summarise(
    planned = n(),
    task_successes = sum(task_pass),
    behavior_successes = sum(behavior_pass),
    confirmation_failures = sum(confirmation_failure),
    errors = sum(status == "error"),
    missing = sum(status == "missing"),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(task_percent = 100 * task_successes / planned)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  scores,
  digits = 1,
  col.names = c(
    "Version", "Planned", "Task success", "Full behavior success",
    "Confirmation failures", "Errors", "Missing", "Task %"
  ),
  caption = "Task success improves, but B skips one required confirmation."
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(scores$version_id, c("A", "B")),
  identical(scores$planned, c(16L, 16L)),
  identical(scores$task_successes, c(10L, 12L)),
  identical(scores$behavior_successes, c(10L, 11L)),
  identical(scores$confirmation_failures, c(0L, 1L)),
  identical(scores$errors, c(1L, 2L)),
  identical(scores$missing, c(0L, 1L)),
  identical(scores$task_percent, c(62.5, 75))
)
```

A meets the task target in 10 of 16 planned trials.
B meets it in 12 of 16.
The increase is 12.5 percentage points.
A **percentage-point change** subtracts one percentage from another.
Here, 75 minus 62.5 equals 12.5.
Full behavior also requires confirmation when the case calls for it.
B meets that combined requirement in 11 of 16 trials.

The `coalesce()` calls replace absent values for these counts only.
They do not change a saved response or grade.
An unknown confirmation is not proof that the system followed the rule.
Errors and missing results will still block approval.

## Inspect the required step

B reaches the requested state in c06, trial 1.
Predict which labels you need to check before you accept that result.

```{r}
confirmation_check <- results |>
  filter(case_id == "c06", version_id == "B", trial_id == 1L) |>
  select(target, response, task_met, confirmed, behavior_pass, judge_pass)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  confirmation_check,
  col.names = c(
    "Requirement", "Invented response", "Task met", "Confirmed",
    "Full behavior met", "Grader passed"
  ),
  caption = "A correct end state can still break the required process."
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  nrow(confirmation_check) == 1L,
  confirmation_check$task_met,
  !confirmation_check$confirmed,
  !confirmation_check$behavior_pass,
  confirmation_check$judge_pass
)
```

Do not accept this result. The author label says the requested state was reached.
The confirmation label says the required step was skipped.
The saved grader missed that failure.
Checking only the final state would also miss it.

## Check the grader

A **false pass** occurs when a grader passes a result that fails the requirement.
A **false fail** occurs when it rejects a result that meets the requirement.
The c02 requirement is "`r sub("[.]$", "", cases$target[cases$case_id == "c02"])`".
Predict whether "You can cancel at no cost" meets that requirement.
The response uses different words.

Audit only completed results with both labels.
The task score kept 32 planned slots.
This audit has 28 completed results because errors and missing results have no
grader verdict.
We leave them out of this audit only. They stay in the task score.

```{r}
audit <- results |>
  filter(status == "completed") |>
  mutate(
    grader_error = case_when(
      judge_pass & !behavior_pass ~ "False pass",
      !judge_pass & behavior_pass ~ "False fail",
      .default = "Agrees with author"
    )
  )

grader_errors <- audit |>
  filter(grader_error != "Agrees with author") |>
  select(case_id, version_id, trial_id, target, response, grader_error)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  grader_errors,
  col.names = c(
    "Case", "Version", "Trial", "Requirement", "Invented response", "Grader error"
  ),
  caption = "Two false passes and one false fail in the invented labels."
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  nrow(audit) == 28L,
  nrow(grader_errors) == 3L,
  sum(audit$grader_error == "False pass") == 2L,
  sum(audit$grader_error == "False fail") == 1L,
  sum(audit$grader_error == "Agrees with author") == 25L
)
```

The paraphrase meets the requirement. Its saved grader label is a false fail.
The other errors pass a reversed meaning and a skipped confirmation.
A valid answer need not match one reference string.
A valid tool sequence need not match one reference path.
Check the required behavior instead.

These invented disagreements show how to inspect a grader.
They do not measure a real grader's accuracy.
For real work, use independent human review and keep disagreements visible.
If a model grades answers, swap the answer order and check its verdict.
Also check whether a longer answer changes its verdict without improving the answer.
A different judge model alone does not prove that its scores are valid.

## Compare each case

A **regression** is a result that gets worse in a new version.
What would you check to find a case that gets worse?
Write your answer before you run the code.
Compare the same cases, with two planned trials per version.
This is a **paired comparison** because A and B use the same cases.

```{r}
paired <- results |>
  group_by(case_id, version_id) |>
  summarise(task_rate = mean(task_pass), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = version_id, values_from = task_rate) |>
  mutate(change = B - A)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  paired,
  digits = 2,
  col.names = c("Case", "A task rate", "B task rate", "B minus A"),
  caption = "B improves on two cases, ties on five, and gets worse on one."
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(paired$change, c(0, 0, 1, 0.5, 0, 0, 0, -0.5)),
  sum(paired$change > 0) == 2L,
  sum(paired$change == 0) == 5L,
  sum(paired$change < 0) == 1L,
  mean(paired$change) == 0.125
)
```

B does not improve on every case.
It fixes c03 and improves c04, but it gets worse on c08.
B has an error in c08, trial 1, and no saved row for trial 2.
Neither trial earns a success.
The average change is 0.125, or 12.5 percentage points.
It describes this fixed example only.
Two attempts at one case are not two independent user situations.
They do not show how the system works for real users.

## Apply the rule

The average task score rises.
The confirmation failure is still present.
Predict the decision before you run this function.

```{r}
release_decision <- function(scores) {
  if (scores$confirmation_failures[scores$version_id == "B"] > 0L) {
    return("Do not release")
  }
  if (any(scores$errors + scores$missing > 0L)) {
    return("Inconclusive")
  }
  rates <- setNames(scores$task_successes / scores$planned, scores$version_id)
  if (rates[["B"]] > rates[["A"]]) {
    return("Passes this demonstration rule")
  }
  "Inconclusive"
}

decision <- release_decision(scores)
decision
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(identical(decision, "Do not release"))
```

Do not release B.
The first rule blocks it because it skipped confirmation.
It also has errors and a missing result.
Those problems would make the decision inconclusive even without the
confirmation failure.
More correct task answers cannot cancel a forbidden action.

## Check your understanding

If you change the failed confirmation label to `TRUE`, can B pass?
Keep all other labels and rows the same.

::: {.callout-note}
## Answer

No. Errors and a missing result remain.
The rule returns "Inconclusive."
Changing a label is not a repair to a real system.
You would need to fix the system and run a new, recorded evaluation.
:::

If all B results were absent, would zero observed confirmation failures prove
that it followed the rule?

::: {.callout-note}
## Answer

No. You have no evidence of its behavior.
Keep all 16 planned B slots and mark them missing.
The decision remains inconclusive.
:::

## What to remember

Compare the same planned cases.
Keep errors and missing results visible.
Check what a score measures before you use it.
A required action and a correct answer are different checks.
Use the release rule you wrote before you saw the results.

Return to [Beyond the periodic table](index.qmd) for the tool distinctions.
This lesson does not execute LangChain, LangGraph, LangSmith, ellmer, or vitals.

## Sources

- [CheckList](https://aclanthology.org/2020.acl-main.442/) motivates tests of
  specific behavior alongside aggregate scores.
- [tau-bench](https://arxiv.org/html/2406.12045v1), section 3, describes checks
  of final state and notes that these can miss required confirmation.
- [Judging LLM-as-a-Judge](https://arxiv.org/html/2306.05685v4), sections 3-4,
  studies answer-order and verbosity effects. Its results do not validate
  the invented grader on this page.
- [RAGAs](https://aclanthology.org/2024.eacl-demo.16/) distinguishes contextual
  support from answer relevance. These are different evaluation targets.

The repository's `DATA_SOURCES.md` records the invented files and their limits.
The data are in `data/system-evaluation/`.
No platform comparison is made.
